British Motor Show 2026: The New EVs That Surprised Me

The British Motor Show 2026 brought together some of the latest electric cars and upcoming EVs heading to the UK. I went hands-on with the Leapmotor B05, Hyundai IONIQ 3, Honda Super-N, Aion UT, Alpine A290 and more to see which impressed, disappointed and genuinely surprised me.

  • 7 min read

Last week I went along to this year’s British Motor Show to check out some of the latest electric cars and upcoming EVs heading to UK roads. If you’ve never been, it’s a bit of everything. There are classics, supercars, modified cars, owners’ clubs, monster truck rides, sim racing and plenty of manufacturer stands. Most of the show is outside, so the fact I picked a hot and sunny day definitely helped, although there are a few indoor halls where you can escape the heat and spend more time looking around some of the newer cars.

That was really the main reason I went this year. My current CUPRA Born EV lease is coming to an end later this year, and I’m now properly looking at what replaces it. There are plenty of new electric cars I’ve read about, written about or watched videos on, but until you actually sit inside one, shut the door and start poking around the cabin, you don’t really know whether you like it. Sadly, not every manufacturer was at the show, but Ford and BYD both had large displays, and there were still enough interesting new EVs inside the main hall to make the trip worthwhile.

Ford Puma Gen-E – It Was Just OK

Ford had one of the bigger outdoor areas and was also offering test drives. I’ve already been inside the new Ford Capri and driven the Ford Explorer EV, so the Puma Gen-E was the one I wanted to see properly. My reaction was fairly simple: it was fine. I wasn’t particularly impressed by the interior quality, and I’m still not a fan of Ford’s vertically shaped steering wheel. That might sound like a small thing, but you’re holding it every time you drive the car, so it matters to me. Nothing about the Puma Gen-E made me think I needed to add it to my shortlist.

I also jumped back into the Ford Mustang Mach-E and had another play with its huge portrait display. I’ve never really loved that setup and still don’t understand the need for such a tall screen in the middle of the dashboard. The one at the show was also a bit glitchy while I was using it, which didn’t exactly help its case.

BYD and Denza – Big Screens and Plenty of Bling

BYD had another large presence at the show, including models from its more upmarket Denza brand. The Denza interiors certainly aren’t subtle, with huge screens, lots of glossy surfaces and plenty of visual drama. The screens themselves were very responsive, though, and it’s clear BYD is happy to put technology right at the centre of the experience.

I also had a look at the BYD Dolphin G hybrid, which is a nice size in person and has an interior that felt instantly familiar after driving the smaller BYD Dolphin Surf earlier this year. BYD now has a very recognisable cabin style, and whether you like that style or not, you can usually tell what you’re sitting in fairly quickly. One issue: it isn’t an EV.

Honda Super-N – My Biggest Disappointment

The Honda Super-N was one I had really wanted to see. I liked the original Honda e, not because it made much financial sense, but because Honda was willing to do something different with it. The Super-N looked as though it might capture some of that same odd little-car character at a more sensible price.

Visually, it does have some personality, but once I started opening the doors and having a proper look around, the shine came off it quite quickly. The doors felt clunky, the boot did too, and the whole thing felt cheaper than I was expecting from Honda. I kept poking around because I thought maybe my first impression would change, but it didn’t. Price will obviously matter a lot, but there are already some strong small EVs around, and unless Honda gets the numbers right, I’d struggle to choose this over some of them.

Alpine A290, Renault 5 and Nissan Micra EV

All three versions of the Renault 5 EV platform were at the show: the Renault 5 itself, the new Nissan Micra EV and the Alpine A290. Of the three, I still think the Alpine is easily the best-looking. It has more presence, and after finally getting inside one, I also preferred the cabin. The gear selector is down in the middle console, taking one of the many stalks away from behind the wheel. It feels more focused around the driver and generally more like something I’d actually want to spend time in.

Then I climbed into the back and was reminded of the same issue that puts me off the whole platform. Rear space really isn’t good. If you rarely carry anyone in the back, it probably won’t matter much, but if those seats are going to be used regularly, I’d definitely try one before committing. It’s a shame because there’s a lot I like about these cars. Ford is expected to use the same basic underpinnings for its future electric Fiesta in 2028, and I hope it can do something about the rear space because I’d happily trade a bit of boot capacity for more room in the back. Maybe even taking the Hyundai Insta/KIA EV2 sliding rear bench design as a good compromise.

Renault Twingo EV – Better Looking in Person

The new Renault Twingo EV was also at the show, and I was pleased to finally see one in the metal. From some of the photos I’d seen, I thought it might look a bit tall and narrow, but it actually sits lower than I expected and looks much better in person.

Unfortunately, Renault had locked the whole thing, so I couldn’t get inside and get a feel for what the interior was actually like. That was frustrating because it’s the part I was most interested in. I’m also keeping an eye on the Twingo because Dacia will use the same platform for the next-generation of its Spring EV, and that could end up being a very interesting, cheap electric car if they get the design and pricing right.

Linktour Alumi – A Very Cheap Electric City Car

One of the stranger cars at the show came from Linktour, a new Chinese brand I hadn’t spent much time looking at before. It brought along the Alumi and Alumi Pro, with both cars available to sit inside. The Alumi is expected to cost somewhere around €10,000, and once you sit in it, that figure makes sense.

It feels cheap, but not in a way that surprised me. The materials are basic, and the build quality feels basic, but this isn’t pretending to be anything premium. It’s a tiny two-seater with some storage behind the seats, a small battery and roughly 100-120 miles of expected range. The closest thing it reminded me of was the Smart EQ Fortwo: a genuinely small electric car designed mainly for getting around town. If the price really does land where people are saying, I can see the appeal.

Hyundai IONIQ 3 – I Expected to Like It More

The Hyundai IONIQ 3 was probably one of the electric cars I was most interested in seeing, especially as the matte red car on display looked great from the outside. Once I got inside, though, I came away a bit underwhelmed. There’s plenty of room, rear space is very good and the packaging is clearly clever, but I didn’t particularly like the way the dashboard sat in front of me. It felt high, and the cabin felt darker than I expected.

This was a left-hand-drive car, so I’m not writing the whole thing off after a few minutes at a motor show, but first impressions are first impressions. One thing I did like was the boot, which is enormous. That front-wheel-drive setup seems to help massively with packaging, and I noticed the same thing on the Volkswagen ID. Polo, and when I drove the CUPRA Raval a few months ago. The practical side of the IONIQ 3 makes a lot of sense; I’m just not sure the rest of it clicked with me straight away.

Aion UT – Good Inside, Boring Outside

The Aion UT was one of those cars where the outside and inside gave me completely different reactions. This small B-segment EV will be going up against cars such as the Renault 5, BYD Dolphin, Mini Electric, Peugeot e208, Volkswagen ID. Polo and Vauxhall Corsa Electric, and inside I thought it was pretty good. There’s loads of space for its size, the technology looks modern, and everything felt reasonably well thought out.

The exterior is where I struggle. A lot of newer Chinese EVs seem to have this same rounded, smooth and very safe-looking design language. Nothing is particularly wrong with it, but nothing grabs me either, and the Aion UT falls into that camp. It isn’t ugly; I just find it anonymous. Hopefully, as these brands get more established in Europe, we’ll see them get a bit braver with the styling because underneath that rather generic exterior there seems to be a decent car.

Leapmotor B05 – My Biggest Surprise

The Leapmotor B05 was probably the biggest surprise of the British Motor Show for me. I’m still not sold on the exterior. There’s something vaguely late Volkswagen Scirocco-like about the shape, but it has that same soft, rounded look that a lot of Chinese EVs are using. Let’s say I wouldn’t turn around in a car park to look at one.

Then I opened the door, and my opinion changed quite a bit. It felt much roomier than I expected; the materials were VERY good, the screens looked good, and the general finish was noticeably better than I had pictured beforehand. I ended up staying in it longer than I planned to, which is usually a decent sign.

This is the sort of thing I think established manufacturers need to pay attention to. If someone can step out of a Volkswagen Golf, Vauxhall Astra or similar C-segment hatchback and into something like this, then find loads of technology, plenty of space and an interior that doesn’t feel cheap, the badge on the front starts doing less work, especially if the price is lower.

I’m still not convinced by the way the standard B05 looks, but interestingly, Leapmotor has already shown a sportier version in China. Over there, the B05 is known as the Lafa 5, and the new Lafa 5 Ultra gets a much more aggressive body kit, larger wheels and sharper styling. Having seen that version since visiting the show, it’s much closer to what I’d personally want the B05 to look like. Sadly, the Ultra is currently intended for the Chinese market, but if Leapmotor eventually brings something similar to the UK, I’d definitely be interested in driving one. The standard B05 surprised me enough inside; give me that interior wrapped in the Ultra’s styling, and it becomes a much more interesting car.

My British Motor Show 2026 EV Highlights

The show was useful for exactly the reason I hoped it would be. Some cars went up in my estimation and some went down. The Honda Super-N was probably my biggest disappointment because I wanted to like it, but it simply felt too cheap to me. The Hyundai IONIQ 3 didn’t click straight away either, while the Alpine A290 was almost exactly what I expected: great-looking, nice inside and not very good in the back.

The Aion UT was much better inside than its fairly anonymous exterior suggests, but the Leapmotor B05 was the new EV that caught me out the most. I still don’t like the way it looks, but the interior was so much better than I expected that I left the show wanting to spend more time with it.

That is really why I like going to events like the British Motor Show. You can read every spec sheet, watch every review and stare at press photos for weeks, but sometimes you just need to sit in the thing, shut the door, mess around with the screen and see whether it actually feels right.

My search for my next EV still isn’t finished. Next up is the Everything Electric Show in London this week, where I’m hoping to get hands-on with a few more new electric cars before my current CUPRA Born goes back later this year.

At some point, I suppose I’m going to have to actually choose one.
